lesson_title: Two Front Doors: Why Redress Exists
hook_text: Same street. Same effort. One family owns their front door — the other was forbidden to.
clip_script: Two young people, both twenty-two, apply for the same junior post in town. The first borrows his mother's car, prints his CV at home, and mentions that his uncle knows the manager. The second wakes at four, takes two taxis paid for with borrowed money, and knows nobody inside any building in that town. Same post. Same interview. Different starting lines. And here's the economics: those lines weren't drawn by effort or by chance. For most of a century, the law drew them. The law said who could own a house — and who could only rent with no title deed. The law said whose school got laboratories. The law said which families lived near the factories and which were moved two taxi rides away. Scrapping those rules did not scrap their results: the house never bought still can't be borrowed against; the trade never taught still can't be passed on. Advantage is inherited — through property, schooling, contacts and address. That's why equal laws and an equal economy are two different things. Closing the distance between them has a name: redress.
visual_style: Split screen of two morning routines — car keys lifted versus coins counted for taxi fare; a street of houses where some doors carry title deeds and others fade to rented outlines; a family tree passing down a house, a certificate and a phone book of contacts on one side, and empty frames on the other.
mood: Calm, factual, humane — no blame, no comfort, just the mechanism laid bare.
pacing: Parallel storytelling at the open, a firm single beat on the law drawing the lines, measured landing on the inheritance point.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to judge redress with both ledgers open.
